paper.title: The effect of job loss on labor supply, wealth, and spousal labor supply for older workers
paper.code_data_availability: Data availability: 'I thank the ECONAU project database (Department of Economics and Business Economics, Aarhus University) for making their data available to me. …

registers.name_in_paper: high-quality Danish administrative data containing the full population of employer-employee matches
registers.role: sample frame; treatment (job loss due to mass layoff); labor market outcomes for workers, partners and adult children; demographics and family links
outcomes: net wealth (excluding pension wealth), assets (excluding pension wealth), liabilities and homeownership; income measures
outcomes (robustness): replication of the wealth results including pension wealth and a detailed decomposition of assets and liabilities (Tables A.5 and A.6)

registers.name_in_paper: RAS1 and RAS202 from Statistics Denmark
registers.role: motivation only: own calculation of the share of the workforce aged 60 to 64 over the last 40 years

registers.name_in_paper: the Consumer Price Index (CPI) from Statistics Denmark
registers.role: deflator: all monetary values adjusted to DKK, 2024-prices
matching/controls: three industry groups (manufacturing, services, other industries)

registers.name_in_paper: the ECONAU project database (Department of Economics and Business Economics, Aarhus University)
registers.role: data access: the project database through which the Danish register data were made available

linkages: individuals can be linked to partners and other family members, so partners' and adult children's labor market outcomes and characteristics are observed
workers are linked to establishments through their main employer, defined as the most important connection to the labor market per end of November

each treated household is linked to one comparison household by 1:1 nearest-neighbour propensity score matching without replacement; matched comparison households are assigned a placebo displacement base year

sample.universe: Danish households in base years 2013-2017 in which (1) the worker is aged 25 to 64 and, one year before the base year, (2) the couple has been married or cohabitating at least two years and (3) the worker has at least two years tenure at a private establishment with at least 20 employees
sample.unit_of_observation: household-year (an event-time panel of households from five years before to five years after the actual or placebo displacement base year t*)
selection_rules: Base years 2013-2017; outcomes observed 2008-2022 (2008 onward for data quality, 2022 the latest year available)
Worker aged 25 to 64 at the base year
Couple married or cohabitating for at least two years one year before the base year
Worker has at least two years of tenure at a private establishment with at least 20 employees
Treated: worker experiences a job loss due to a mass layoff (establishment employment falls by more than 30% in t* and the worker separates from the main employer)
Displacement events where more than 20% of workers move jointly to another firm are excluded (to exclude mergers and outsourcing)
Treated workers re-employed at their pre-job-loss main employer after the job loss are dropped
Households where the worker has experienced a job loss before are removed, so only treated and never-treated households are compared
Comparison workers may work at mass-layoff establishments as long as they are not displaced themselves, and may separate for other reasons than a mass layoff
Households where the partner loses their job are excluded, to avoid common shocks

1:1 nearest-neighbour propensity score matching without replacement: exact matching on displacement base year, one-year age bins, gender and spousal status (partner aged 60 or above at t*), then propensity score matching on partner's age, years together with partner, children dummy, full-time dummy, industry groups, tenure, employer size, local labor market unemployment rate and worker's earnings in t*-2 and t*-3
Older workers: workers aged 60 to 64 at the base year; older partners: partners aged 60 or older at t* (60% of the older-worker sample); younger partners: partners under 60 at t* (40%)
For the older-partner analysis, partners are split by whether they were employed in t*-3
sample.n_observations: 69,954 household-year observations for older workers (Tables 2, 3 and 5); 30,119 for older partners previously employed (Table 4)
sample.n_individuals: 6506 individuals for older workers (Table 1 reports 3253 treated and 3253 comparison households); 2791 for older partners previously employed

construction_notes: All monetary values are adjusted to DKK, 2024-prices, using the Consumer Price Index (CPI) from Statistics Denmark (1 DKK is approximately 0.14 USD)

Earnings is the sum of annual labor earnings before taxation and includes overtime, bonuses and severance payments; winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentile; set to 0 for individuals without earnings
All wealth and income measures are winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentile

Labor market attachment: six mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive groups based on the main source of income at the end of November (employment, transfers, disability pension, self-supporting, early retirement, state pension)

Disposable income is total income after taxes and interest expenses with the calculated rental value of own home added; total personal income is the sum of all labor earnings, public transfers, capital income and all other non-classifiable income
Non-public pension income is pension income from occupational and private pensions; studied both on the extensive margin and as an amount in DKK
For older partners, early retirement and state pension benefits are bundled into one category, public pension benefits, to increase power

Mass layoff: employment drops by more than 30% in t* at the establishment of the worker's main employment in t*-1 and the worker separates from the main employer in t*; the definition includes plant closures; only private establishments with at least 20 employees are considered
The coefficients of interest are normalised relative to the coefficient three years before the displacement base year
Standard errors are clustered at the household level
Liquidity constraints are defined as household assets lower than monthly household disposable income in t*-3
Three industry groups are defined from Danish DB07 industry groups (10-groupings): manufacturing, services, other industries
Local labor markets follow the definition of Statistics Denmark (2016)

claims.statement: For older workers (aged 60 to 64 at displacement), job loss due to a mass layoff changes employment by -0.264 one year after the displacement event.

treatment.label: Job loss due to mass layoff (displacement)

definition.value: Treatedi = 1 for households where the worker experiences a job loss due to a mass layoff: employment drops by more than 30% in the displacement base year t* at the establishment where the worker had their main employment in t*-1, and the worker separates from their main employer in t*. Displacement events where more than 20% of workers move jointly to another firm are excluded, treated workers re-employed at their pre-job-loss main employer are dropped, and only private establishments with at least 20 employees are considered. Comparison households are never-treated households matched 1:1 by nearest-neighbour propensity score and assigned a placebo base year.

timing.value: Displacement base year t*, one of 2013-2017; outcomes are followed from five years before to five years after t*

definition.value: One of six mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive labor market attachment groups, defined from the main source of income at the end of November; Employment is an indicator variable for being employed

timing.value: Measured in each year of the household panel (annual register data) relative to the displacement base year t*; the reported coefficient is the effect measured one year after the displacement event

units.value: change in the probability of the outcome (0-1 scale; 0.01 = 1 percentage point)

magnitude.interpretation: the large decrease in employment of 26 pp.

estimand.target_population: Households whose worker is displaced in a mass layoff (the treated households), i.e. the effect of job loss for those who lose their job
estimand.time_horizon: one year after the displacement event

population.description: Households in which the worker is aged 60 to 64 at the displacement base year t* ('older workers'): treated households whose worker is displaced in a mass layoff plus their 1:1 propensity-score-matched never-treated comparison households
population.ages: 60 to 64 at the displacement base year t*
subgroups_defined: workers aged 60 to 64 vs five-year age bins from 25-29 up to 55-59
younger partners (under 60 at t*) vs older partners (aged 60 or older at t*)
older partners employed in t*-3 vs not employed in t*-3
men vs women
population.selection: Households observed in base years 2013-2017 where the worker is aged 25 to 64, the couple has been married or cohabitating for at least two years and the worker has at least two years of tenure at a private establishment with at least 20 employees; households where the worker had experienced a job loss before are removed, and households where the partner loses their job are excluded; comparison households are matched 1:1 on the propensity score

identification.source_of_variation: Involuntary job separation in a mass layoff: employment at the establishment of the worker's main employment drops by more than 30% in the displacement base year t* (2013-2017) and the worker separates from that employer; private establishments with at least 20 employees; treated households matched 1:1 by propensity score to never-treated households

key_assumptions.assumption: Common trends: treated and matched comparison households would have followed parallel trends in the outcome in the absence of job loss
key_assumptions.supported_by: Pre-displacement trends in the event study framework (Figs. 2, 4, 6, 7 and Fig. A.6 show pre-period coefficients; the text states that displaced and non-displaced workers are alike before job loss)

key_assumptions.assumption: Job loss in a mass layoff is driven by firm-level shocks rather than by the worker's own (unobserved) characteristics, so that after propensity-score matching and household and year fixed effects displacement is as good as randomly assigned
key_assumptions.supported_by: Mass-layoff definition; 1:1 nearest-neighbour propensity-score matching; Table 1 balance of treated and comparison households; household fixed effects absorbing time-invariant observed and unobserved characteristics

rhs: Household time-invariant observed and unobserved characteristics

implies_edges.to: Job loss due to mass layoff (displacement)

implies_edges.from: Household time-invariant observed and unobserved characteristics
implies_edges.to: Employment (probability of being employed)

key_assumptions.assumption: No anticipation: the displacement does not affect outcomes before the base year, so pre-displacement years (coefficients are normalised relative to three years before the event) are untreated
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table A.7 shows that average earnings, age, share of male workers and establishment size do not change significantly from five years to one year before the mass layoff; robustness check allowing separations in the year before the mass layoff (Fig. A.16); normalisation relative to the coefficient three years before the event; spousal pre-employment measured in t*-3 to avoid anticipation

implies_edges.from: Job loss due to mass layoff (displacement)
implies_edges.to: Employment (probability of being employed) (pre-displacement years)

key_assumptions.assumption: No common shock to the household: households in which the partner also loses their job are excluded from the sample, so the estimated spillovers are not driven by correlated shocks
key_assumptions.supported_by: Sample exclusion of households where the partner loses their job; robustness check excluding couples working at the same establishment the year before displacement (Table A.8)

implies_edges.from: Partner's own job loss
implies_edges.to: Inclusion in the estimation sample

key_assumptions.assumption: Overlap / comparability: each treated household has a comparable never-treated household on the matching characteristics
key_assumptions.supported_by: Table 1 summary statistics show no statistically significant differences between treated and comparison older-worker households except the services-industry dummy (p = 0.08)

threats_discussed: Comparison households may differ from displaced households along unobservable dimensions, e.g. sorting into more stable firms or selective retention during downsizing episodes
Anticipation of the mass layoff, so that workers remaining at the establishment the year before the layoff are a selected group
The COVID-19 pandemic may have affected workers aged 60 and above differentially
Common shocks to both partners in a couple
Endogenous choice of switching industry after displacement
Small sample of about 6500 older workers (about 30% female), limiting power in subgroup analyses
robustness_checks: Excluding the years 2020-2022 (COVID-19 pandemic), Appendix A.3
Effects estimated separately by displacement year, Appendix A.4
Exact balancing on partner's employment status and spousal earnings in t*-3 when matching (Fig. A.15)
Allowing separations to happen in t*-1 as well as in the displacement base year (Fig. A.16)
Excluding couples working at the same establishment the year before displacement (Table A.8)
Repeating the analysis for the full population of singles and couples, Appendix A.5
Restricting to private establishments with 30 or more employees, Appendix A.6
Replicating the wealth results with the more detailed Wealth Register (FORMPERS), Table A.5
unresolved_confounders: Unobservable differences between displaced and comparison households, e.g. sorting into more stable firms or selective retention during downsizing episodes
Whether the results are driven by labor demand or labor supply factors cannot be definitively distinguished
Selection of the workers who remain at the establishment until the layoff year (the robustness check allowing separations in t*-1 gives smaller effects)
Endogeneity of industry switching and of participation in the VERP early-retirement scheme

estimation.specification: Eq. (1): event study with household and year fixed effects, event-time indicators and event-time x Treated interactions, coefficients normalised relative to the coefficient three years before the base year; estimated on the matched panel of treated and comparison households; the reported coefficient is the one-year effect
controls: 1:1 nearest-neighbour propensity-score matching (no replacement) on pre-displacement characteristics

adjustment_set.label: event-time indicators (years relative to the displacement base year)

propensity-score matching covariates: partner's age, number of years together with partner, dummy for children, dummy for working full time, industry groups, worker's tenure, worker's employer size, local labor market unemployment rate, worker's earnings in t*-2 and t*-3; exact matching on base year, one-year age bins, gender and whether the partner is aged 60 or above

mediators_claimed: take-up of early retirement benefits and state pension benefits, i.e. labor market exit through public pension programs
availability of early retirement benefits (VERP) discouraging job search following displacement
low probability of re-employment for older workers

heterogeneity.dimension: Eligibility for early retirement benefits (contributions to the VERP scheme by age 55)
heterogeneity.finding: Individuals eligible for early retirement benefits experience larger short-run employment losses (28 pp.) than individuals who have not contributed to the scheme (21 pp.); the difference is not statistically significant due to large confidence intervals (Fig. A.13)
Workers whose partners are not employed experience larger employment losses (30 pp.) than those with partners employed (25 pp.), although the difference is not statistically significant
Individuals with low education experience larger employment losses (28 pp.) than highly educated individuals (22 pp.)
The employment loss one year after job loss is 26 pp. for workers aged 60 to 64, 12 pp. for workers aged 55 to 59 and 5 pp. for workers aged 30 to 34

heterogeneity.dimension: Distance to the state pension eligibility age
heterogeneity.finding: Earnings and employment losses following job loss are larger, the shorter the distance to the state pension eligibility age (Fig. A.7)

links.pointer_quote: The first year after job loss, displaced older workers earn 32% less, face a 13% loss in disposable income, and are 26 percentage points (pp.) less likely to be employed than non-displaced workers.

anchor_quote.text: One year after job loss, the large decrease in employment of 26 pp. is almost counteracted by the large increase in the probability of being on early retirement benefits of 16 pp. for older workers.

definition.value: Treatedi = 1 for households where the worker experiences a job loss due to a mass layoff: employment drops by more than 30% in the displacement base year t* at the establishment where the worker had their main employment in t*-1, and the worker separates from their main employer in t*. mediators_claimed: state pension benefits depending on spousal labor income during the sample period, creating financial incentives for joint retirement
leisure complementarities, i.e. a preference for spending time together in retirement

heterogeneity.finding: For older partners not employed in t*-3 there are no spousal labor supply effects, while for those employed in t*-3 the effect is clearly negative (Fig. 7)
There is some suggestive evidence that partners who are secondary earners are more likely to exit employment and enter retirement following displacement (Fig. A.14)

Estimates for liquidity-constrained couples are imprecise with wide confidence intervals and the point estimate for employment is even positive, suggesting the retirement of older partners is primarily driven by couples that are not liquidity constrained
For older partners employed pre-job loss, the effect is driven by female spouses in the short run (Fig. A.12, panel c)
The five-year effect on spousal labor supply is no longer statistically significant while the one-year effect persists
